sections.heading: Part I — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Foundational Fluency (1–7)

questions.q: Find the determinant of the matrix with rows $\langle4,3\rangle,\langle2,5\rangle$.
Find the determinant of the matrix with rows $\langle1,2,3\rangle,\langle0,1,4\rangle,\langle5,6,0\rangle$ by cofactor expansion along the first row.
questions.answer: $1\det(\langle1,4\rangle,\langle6,0\rangle)-2\det(\langle0,4\rangle,\langle5,0\rangle)+3\det(\langle0,1\rangle,\langle5,6\rangle) = 1(0-24)-2(0-20)+3(0-5) = -24+40-15=1$.
questions.explanation: $1\det(\langle1,4\rangle,\langle6,0\rangle)-2\det(\langle0,4\rangle,\langle5,0\rangle)+3\det(\langle0,1\rangle,\langle5,6\rangle) = 1(0-24)-2(0-20)+3(0-5) = -24+40-15=1$.

questions.q: Recompute the determinant of the matrix with rows $\langle1,2,3\rangle,\langle0,1,4\rangle,\langle5,6,0\rangle$ by expanding along the SECOND row instead, to confirm the answer matches.
questions.answer: Expanding along row 2 (with alternating signs $-,+,-$): $-0\det(\langle2,3\rangle,\langle6,0\rangle)+1\det(\langle1,3\rangle,\langle5,0\rangle)-4\det(\langle1,2\rangle,\langle5,6\rangle) = 0+1(0-15)-4(6-10) = -15+16=1$. Matches the earlier result of $1$.
questions.explanation: Expanding along row 2 (with alternating signs $-,+,-$): $-0\det(\langle2,3\rangle,\langle6,0\rangle)+1\det(\langle1,3\rangle,\langle5,0\rangle)-4\det(\langle1,2\rangle,\langle5,6\rangle) = 0+1(0-15)-4(6-10) = -15+16=1$. Matches the earlier result of $1$.

questions.q: For $A$ with rows $\langle1,2\rangle,\langle3,4\rangle$ and $B$ with rows $\langle2,1\rangle,\langle0,3\rangle$, verify $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$.
questions.answer: $\det A=4-6=-2$, $\det B=6-0=6$, so $\det A\det B=-12$. $AB$ has rows $\langle2,7\rangle,\langle6,15\rangle$ (computed as usual matrix multiplication), and $\det(AB)=2(15)-7(6)=30-42=-12$. They match.
questions.explanation: $\det A=4-6=-2$, $\det B=6-0=6$, so $\det A\det B=-12$. $AB$ has rows $\langle2,7\rangle,\langle6,15\rangle$ (computed as usual matrix multiplication), and $\det(AB)=2(15)-7(6)=30-42=-12$. They match.

questions.q: Using the product rule $\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)$, explain why $\det(A^{-1})=\frac{1}{\det A}$ for an invertible matrix $A$.
questions.answer: Since $AA^{-1}=I$ and $\det I=1$, the product rule gives $\det(A)\det(A^{-1})=1$. Dividing both sides by $\det A$ (nonzero since $A$ is invertible) gives $\det(A^{-1})=\frac{1}{\det A}$.
questions.explanation: Since $AA^{-1}=I$ and $\det I=1$, the product rule gives $\det(A)\det(A^{-1})=1$. Dividing both sides by $\det A$ (nonzero since $A$ is invertible) gives $\det(A^{-1})=\frac{1}{\det A}$.

questions.q: If $A$ is a $2\times2$ matrix with $\det A=5$, find $\det(2A)$ (scaling EVERY entry of $A$ by $2$).
questions.target: Determinants and scalar multiples / row operations
questions.answer: For an $n\times n$ matrix, $\det(cA)=c^n\det A$. For $n=2$: $\det(2A)=2^2(5)=20$.
questions.explanation: For an $n\times n$ matrix, $\det(cA)=c^n\det A$. For $n=2$: $\det(2A)=2^2(5)=20$.

questions.q: If $A$ is a $3\times3$ matrix with $\det A=5$, find $\det(2A)$.
questions.target: Determinants and scalar multiples / row operations
questions.answer: $\det(2A)=2^3(5)=40$ (note this is different from the $2\times2$ case — the exponent depends on the matrix's size).
questions.explanation: $\det(2A)=2^3(5)=40$ (note this is different from the $2\times2$ case — the exponent depends on the matrix's size).

sections.heading: Part II — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Intermediate Multi-Step Application (8–14)

questions.q: Swapping two rows of a matrix negates its determinant. If $A$ has rows $\langle1,2\rangle,\langle3,4\rangle$ with $\det A=-2$, find the determinant of the matrix with rows swapped: $\langle3,4\rangle,\langle1,2\rangle$.
questions.target: Determinants and scalar multiples / row operations
questions.answer: Swapping rows negates the determinant: $\det=-(-2)=2$. (Direct check: $3(2)-4(1)=6-4=2$.)
questions.explanation: Swapping rows negates the determinant: $\det=-(-2)=2$. (Direct check: $3(2)-4(1)=6-4=2$.)

questions.q: State the invertibility criterion in terms of the determinant.
questions.answer: A square matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $\det A\neq0$.
questions.explanation: A square matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $\det A\neq0$.

questions.q: Is the matrix with rows $\langle2,4\rangle,\langle1,2\rangle$ invertible? Justify using the determinant.
questions.answer: $\det=2(2)-4(1)=0$. Since the determinant is $0$, the matrix is NOT invertible (singular).
questions.explanation: $\det=2(2)-4(1)=0$. Since the determinant is $0$, the matrix is NOT invertible (singular).

questions.q: For what value(s) of $k$ is the matrix with rows $\langle k,2\rangle,\langle3,k\rangle$ NOT invertible?
questions.answer: $\det=k^2-6$. Setting $k^2-6=0$ gives $k=\pm\sqrt{6}$. The matrix fails to be invertible exactly when $k=\sqrt{6}$ or $k=-\sqrt{6}$.
questions.explanation: $\det=k^2-6$. Setting $k^2-6=0$ gives $k=\pm\sqrt{6}$. The matrix fails to be invertible exactly when $k=\sqrt{6}$ or $k=-\sqrt{6}$.

questions.q: For a $2\times2$ matrix $A$ with rows $\mathbf{r}_1,\mathbf{r}_2$, $|\det A|$ gives the area of the parallelogram spanned by $\mathbf{r}_1$ and $\mathbf{r}_2$. Find this area for $\mathbf{r}_1=\langle3,0\rangle$, $\mathbf{r}_2=\langle1,4\rangle$.
Explain, using the geometric meaning of the determinant, why a matrix with two identical rows always has determinant $0$.
questions.answer: Two identical rows span a degenerate "parallelogram" with zero area (the two vectors are parallel, in fact equal, so they don't sweep out any two-dimensional region) — matching $\det=0$.
questions.explanation: Two identical rows span a degenerate "parallelogram" with zero area (the two vectors are parallel, in fact equal, so they don't sweep out any two-dimensional region) — matching $\det=0$.

questions.q: Find the determinant of the identity matrix $I_3$ (rows $\langle1,0,0\rangle,\langle0,1,0\rangle,\langle0,0,1\rangle$).
questions.answer: $\det I_3=1$ (expanding along any row/column, the product of the diagonal entries, all $1$'s, with every off-diagonal cofactor contributing $0$).
questions.explanation: $\det I_3=1$ (expanding along any row/column, the product of the diagonal entries, all $1$'s, with every off-diagonal cofactor contributing $0$).

sections.heading: Part III — Free-Response Questions (FRQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (15–20)

questions.q: Find the determinant of the matrix with rows $\langle3,0,0\rangle,\langle0,-2,0\rangle,\langle0,0,5\rangle$ (a diagonal matrix).
questions.answer: For a diagonal (or more generally triangular) matrix, the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries: $3(-2)(5)=-30$.
questions.explanation: For a diagonal (or more generally triangular) matrix, the determinant is the product of the diagonal entries: $3(-2)(5)=-30$.

questions.q: Find the determinant of the matrix with rows $\langle0,0,3\rangle,\langle0,1,0\rangle,\langle3,0,0\rangle$, and explain why it is nonzero even though the main diagonal has two zeros.
questions.answer: Expanding along row 2 (only nonzero entry is the middle $1$): $\det=1\cdot\det(\langle0,3\rangle,\langle3,0\rangle)=1(0-9)=-9$. The main-diagonal shortcut only applies to TRIANGULAR matrices; this matrix is not triangular (it has nonzero entries above AND below the diagonal), so the diagonal-product rule doesn't apply here.
questions.explanation: Expanding along row 2 (only nonzero entry is the middle $1$): $\det=1\cdot\det(\langle0,3\rangle,\langle3,0\rangle)=1(0-9)=-9$. The main-diagonal shortcut only applies to TRIANGULAR matrices; this matrix is not triangular (it has nonzero entries above AND below the diagonal), so the diagonal-product rule doesn't apply here.

questions.q: Find the determinant of the zero matrix (all entries $0$) of any size, and connect this to the invertibility criterion.
questions.answer: $\det=0$ for the zero matrix of any size (every row is the zero vector, so every cofactor expansion term vanishes). This matches the invertibility criterion: the zero matrix is never invertible.
questions.explanation: $\det=0$ for the zero matrix of any size (every row is the zero vector, so every cofactor expansion term vanishes). This matches the invertibility criterion: the zero matrix is never invertible.

questions.q: Explain why any matrix with an entire row (or column) of zeros must have determinant $0$, using cofactor expansion along that row.
questions.answer: Expanding along a row of all zeros, every term in the cofactor expansion is (zero entry)$\times$(its cofactor)$=0$, so the whole sum is $0$.
questions.explanation: Expanding along a row of all zeros, every term in the cofactor expansion is (zero entry)$\times$(its cofactor)$=0$, so the whole sum is $0$.

questions.q: Cramer's Rule solves $ax+by=e$, $cx+dy=f$ via $x=\frac{\det A_x}{\det A}$, $y=\frac{\det A_y}{\det A}$, where $A$ is the coefficient matrix and $A_x,A_y$ replace the respective column with $\langle e,f\rangle$. Use it to solve $2x+3y=8$, $x-y=1$.
questions.answer: $A$ has rows $\langle2,3\rangle,\langle1,-1\rangle$, $\det A=-2-3=-5$. $A_x$ has rows $\langle8,3\rangle,\langle1,-1\rangle$, $\det A_x=-8-3=-11$, so $x=\frac{-11}{-5}=\frac{11}{5}$. $A_y$ has rows $\langle2,8\rangle,\langle1,1\rangle$, $\det A_y=2-8=-6$, so $y=\frac{-6}{-5}=\frac{6}{5}$.
questions.explanation: $A$ has rows $\langle2,3\rangle,\langle1,-1\rangle$, $\det A=-2-3=-5$. $A_x$ has rows $\langle8,3\rangle,\langle1,-1\rangle$, $\det A_x=-8-3=-11$, so $x=\frac{-11}{-5}=\frac{11}{5}$. $A_y$ has rows $\langle2,8\rangle,\langle1,1\rangle$, $\det A_y=2-8=-6$, so $y=\frac{-6}{-5}=\frac{6}{5}$.

questions.q: Explain why Cramer's Rule fails (gives no unique solution) whenever $\det A=0$.
questions.answer: Division by $\det A=0$ is undefined, and this matches the invertibility criterion: $\det A=0$ means the coefficient matrix is singular, so the system does not have a unique solution (it has either no solution or infinitely many).
questions.explanation: Division by $\det A=0$ is undefined, and this matches the invertibility criterion: $\det A=0$ means the coefficient matrix is singular, so the system does not have a unique solution (it has either no solution or infinitely many).

sections.heading: Part IV — Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQs): Foundational Concept Mastery (21–28)

questions.q: Find the slope of the least-squares line for $\left( -1, \ -1\right)$, $\left( 3, \ 2\right)$, $\left( 4, \ 1\right)$.
questions.answer: Normal equations: $\left[\left(3, 6 ; 6, 26\right)\right]\left[\beta_0 ; \beta_1\right]=\left[2 ; 11\right]$, giving $\hat\beta_0=- \frac{1}{3},\ \hat\beta_1=\frac{1}{2}$.
questions.explanation: Normal equations: $\left[\left(3, 6 ; 6, 26\right)\right]\left[\beta_0 ; \beta_1\right]=\left[2 ; 11\right]$, giving $\hat\beta_0=- \frac{1}{3},\ \hat\beta_1=\frac{1}{2}$.

questions.q: Given $A=\left[\left(-8, 9 ; -6, 7\right)\right]=PDP^{-1}$ with $P=\left[\left(3, 1 ; 2, 1\right)\right]$, $D=\left[\left(-2, 0 ; 0, 1\right)\right]$, find the (2,2) entry of $A^4$.
questions.answer: $A^4=PD^4P^{-1}$ with $D^4=\left[\left(16, 0 ; 0, 1\right)\right]$. Multiplying out, $A^4=\left[\left(46, -45 ; 30, -29\right)\right]$, so the entry is $-29$.
questions.explanation: $A^4=PD^4P^{-1}$ with $D^4=\left[\left(16, 0 ; 0, 1\right)\right]$. Multiplying out, $A^4=\left[\left(46, -45 ; 30, -29\right)\right]$, so the entry is $-29$.

questions.q: Find the distance from the point $\left( 4, \ -1\right)$ to the line through the origin spanned by $\langle 2, -2 \rangle$.
questions.answer: The distance is $||\mathbf{y}-\mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{y}||=||\langle \frac{3}{2}, \frac{3}{2} \rangle||=\frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{2}$.
questions.explanation: The distance is $||\mathbf{y}-\mathrm{proj}_{\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{y}||=||\langle \frac{3}{2}, \frac{3}{2} \rangle||=\frac{3 \sqrt{2}}{2}$.

questions.q: Find the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{y}=\langle -4, -2 \rangle$ onto $\mathbf{u}=\langle 0, 2 \rangle$.
questions.target: Determinants and scalar multiples / row operations
questions.answer: $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\frac{\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u}=\frac{-4}{4}\mathbf{u}=\langle 0, -2 \rangle$.
questions.explanation: $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\frac{\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}}{\mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{u}}\mathbf{u}=\frac{-4}{4}\mathbf{u}=\langle 0, -2 \rangle$.

questions.q: Which vector is an eigenvector of $A=\left[\left(3, -12 ; 2, -7\right)\right]$ for $\lambda = -3$?
questions.answer: Solve $(A--3I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$: $\left[\left(6, -12 ; 2, -4\right)\right]$ has null space spanned by $\langle 2, 1 \rangle$.
questions.explanation: Solve $(A--3I)\mathbf{v}=\mathbf{0}$: $\left[\left(6, -12 ; 2, -4\right)\right]$ has null space spanned by $\langle 2, 1 \rangle$.

questions.q: What is the dimension of $\mathrm{span}\{x^{2} + 1, 2 x^{2} + 2\}$ in $P_2$?
questions.answer: Write each polynomial as a coefficient vector in $\{1,x,x^2\}$ and row-reduce: 1 of them are independent, so the dimension is 1.
questions.explanation: Write each polynomial as a coefficient vector in $\{1,x,x^2\}$ and row-reduce: 1 of them are independent, so the dimension is 1.

questions.q: Find the orthogonal projection of $\langle -1, 4, 3 \rangle$ onto $W=\mathrm{span}\{\langle 1, 0, 1 \rangle, \langle 1, 0, -1 \rangle\}$ (an orthogonal basis).
questions.answer: $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\sum\frac{\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i}{\mathbf{u}_i\cdot\mathbf{u}_i}\mathbf{u}_i=\langle -1, 0, 3 \rangle$.
questions.explanation: $\hat{\mathbf{y}}=\sum\frac{\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i}{\mathbf{u}_i\cdot\mathbf{u}_i}\mathbf{u}_i=\langle -1, 0, 3 \rangle$.

questions.q: Find the characteristic polynomial of $\left[\left(3, -4 ; -4, -2\right)\right]$.
questions.answer: $\det(A-\lambda I)=\lambda^2-(\mathrm{tr}A)\lambda+\det A$ with $\mathrm{tr}A=1$, $\det A=-22$: $\lambda^{2} - \lambda - 22$.
questions.explanation: $\det(A-\lambda I)=\lambda^2-(\mathrm{tr}A)\lambda+\det A$ with $\mathrm{tr}A=1$, $\det A=-22$: $\lambda^{2} - \lambda - 22$.

sections.heading: Part V — Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQs): Intermediate Exam Application (29–37)

questions.q: $\langle 1, 1, 1 \rangle$, $\langle 1, -1, 0 \rangle$, $\langle 1, 1, -2 \rangle$ is an orthogonal basis. Find the coefficient of $\langle 1, 1, -2 \rangle$ when $\langle 5, 2, -5 \rangle$ is written in this basis.
questions.answer: For an orthogonal basis $c_i=\frac{\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i}{\mathbf{u}_i\cdot\mathbf{u}_i}=\frac{17}{6}=\frac{17}{6}$.
questions.explanation: For an orthogonal basis $c_i=\frac{\mathbf{y}\cdot\mathbf{u}_i}{\mathbf{u}_i\cdot\mathbf{u}_i}=\frac{17}{6}=\frac{17}{6}$.

questions.q: $A$ has eigenvalues $2, 3$. What are the eigenvalues of $A+2I$?
questions.answer: If $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}$ then $A+2I$ acts on $\mathbf{v}$ by the same function of $\lambda$, giving $4, 5$.
questions.explanation: If $A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v}$ then $A+2I$ acts on $\mathbf{v}$ by the same function of $\lambda$, giving $4, 5$.

questions.q: Are $\langle 1, 4 \rangle$ and $\langle -2, -8 \rangle$ linearly independent?
choices: Only if one of them is the zero vector
It cannot be decided from the vectors alone
questions.answer: $\det\left[\left(1, -2 ; 4, -8\right)\right]=0$. A zero determinant means one vector is a multiple of the other.
questions.explanation: $\det\left[\left(1, -2 ; 4, -8\right)\right]=0$. A zero determinant means one vector is a multiple of the other.

questions.q: Find the image of $\langle 3, 1 \rangle$ under the reflection across the x-axis.
questions.answer: The standard matrix is $\left[\left(1, 0 ; 0, -1\right)\right]$; multiplying gives $\langle 3, -1 \rangle$.
questions.explanation: The standard matrix is $\left[\left(1, 0 ; 0, -1\right)\right]$; multiplying gives $\langle 3, -1 \rangle$.

questions.q: Find the image of $\langle 1, -2 \rangle$ under the scaling by the factor 3.
questions.target: Determinants and scalar multiples / row operations
questions.answer: The standard matrix is $\left[\left(3, 0 ; 0, 3\right)\right]$; multiplying gives $\langle 3, -6 \rangle$.
questions.explanation: The standard matrix is $\left[\left(3, 0 ; 0, 3\right)\right]$; multiplying gives $\langle 3, -6 \rangle$.

questions.q: Find the image of $\langle -1, 2 \rangle$ under the orthogonal projection onto the x-axis.
questions.answer: The standard matrix is $\left[\left(1, 0 ; 0, 0\right)\right]$; multiplying gives $\langle -1, 0 \rangle$.
questions.explanation: The standard matrix is $\left[\left(1, 0 ; 0, 0\right)\right]$; multiplying gives $\langle -1, 0 \rangle$.

questions.q: Find the image of $\langle 3, 2 \rangle$ under the horizontal shear x ↦ x + 3y.
questions.answer: The standard matrix is $\left[\left(1, 3 ; 0, 1\right)\right]$; multiplying gives $\langle 9, 2 \rangle$.
questions.explanation: The standard matrix is $\left[\left(1, 3 ; 0, 1\right)\right]$; multiplying gives $\langle 9, 2 \rangle$.

questions.q: What is the dimension of $\mathrm{span}$ of $\langle 2, -3, 1 \rangle$, $\langle 2, -3, 1 \rangle$, $\langle 2, -3, 1 \rangle$, $\langle -4, 6, -2 \rangle$?
questions.answer: Row-reduce the matrix with these vectors as rows; it has 1 nonzero row(s), so the span has dimension 1.
questions.explanation: Row-reduce the matrix with these vectors as rows; it has 1 nonzero row(s), so the span has dimension 1.

questions.q: Let $W$ be spanned by $\langle 8, -2, 4, 0, 3 \rangle$, $\langle -2, 0, -2, 0, -3 \rangle$, $\langle -1, 0, -2, -2, 3 \rangle$, $\langle 3, -1, 1, 0, 0 \rangle$ in $R^5$. What is $\dim W^\perp$?
questions.answer: $W^\perp$ is the null space of the matrix with these rows. Its rank is 3, so $\dim W^\perp=5-3=2$.
questions.explanation: $W^\perp$ is the null space of the matrix with these rows. Its rank is 3, so $\dim W^\perp=5-3=2$.

sections.heading: Part VI — Multiple-Choice Questions (MCQs): Challenging & Cross-Lesson Synthesis (38–45)

questions.q: Find the dimension of the null space of $\left[\left(3, 3, -2, 1, -1, -3 ; 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0 ; -3, -3, 2, -1, 1, 3 ; -3, -3, 2, -1, 1, 3\right)\right]$.
questions.answer: Row reduction shows rank 1. By rank–nullity, $\dim\mathrm{Nul}A=n-\mathrm{rank}A=6-1=5$.
questions.explanation: Row reduction shows rank 1. By rank–nullity, $\dim\mathrm{Nul}A=n-\mathrm{rank}A=6-1=5$.

questions.q: What is the dimension of the subspace of $R^4$ defined by $2 x_{1} - x_{2} + 2 x_{3} - 2 x_{4}=0,\ - x_{1} - 3 x_{2} - x_{4}=0$?
questions.answer: The 2 equation(s) are independent (rank 2), so the solution space has dimension $4-2=2$.
questions.explanation: The 2 equation(s) are independent (rank 2), so the solution space has dimension $4-2=2$.

questions.q: Find the eigenvalues of $\left[\left(4, 0 ; 3, 3\right)\right]$.
questions.answer: The matrix is triangular, so its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries: $3, 4$.
questions.explanation: The matrix is triangular, so its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries: $3, 4$.

questions.q: $\mathbf{v}=\langle 4, 6 \rangle$ is an eigenvector of $A=\left[\left(7, -2 ; 6, 0\right)\right]$. What is its eigenvalue?
questions.answer: $A\mathbf{v}=\langle 16, 24 \rangle=4\langle 4, 6 \rangle$, so $\lambda = 4$.
questions.explanation: $A\mathbf{v}=\langle 16, 24 \rangle=4\langle 4, 6 \rangle$, so $\lambda = 4$.

questions.q: $T: R^7 R^5$ is linear with range of dimension 4. What is $\dim\ker T$?
questions.target: Determinants and scalar multiples / row operations
questions.answer: Rank–nullity: $\dim\ker T+\dim\mathrm{range}T=7$, so $\dim\ker T=3$.
questions.explanation: Rank–nullity: $\dim\ker T+\dim\mathrm{range}T=7$, so $\dim\ker T=3$.

questions.q: What is the dimension of $\{A\in M_{2\times2}:\mathrm{tr}A=0\}$?
questions.answer: The dimension is 3: one linear condition removes one dimension.
questions.explanation: The dimension is 3: one linear condition removes one dimension.

questions.q: For which $k$ are $\langle 0, -2, -2 \rangle$ and $\langle -1, 2, k \rangle$ orthogonal?
questions.answer: Set the dot product to zero: $- 2 k - 4=0$, so $k = -2$.
questions.explanation: Set the dot product to zero: $- 2 k - 4=0$, so $k = -2$.

questions.q: $T: R^6 R^4$ is linear with $\dim\ker T=3$. What is the dimension of its range?
questions.answer: Rank–nullity: $\dim\mathrm{range}T=6-3=3$.
questions.explanation: Rank–nullity: $\dim\mathrm{range}T=6-3=3$.
